# HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation

Mingyu Lu1,2∗ Timothy Ossowski2 Tristan Naumann2

1University of Washington 2Microsoft Research 3Recursion mingyulu@cs.washington.edu

## Abstract

Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce HERO (Harnessing Evidence for Refinement and Optimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, HERO learns reusable prompt updates from executionverified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, HERO achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by 7.6 points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another 2.0 points and improves execution eﬀiciency.

## 1 Introduction

LLM agents are increasingly employed to interact with external environments through tools, often by generating executable programs such as SQL and Cypher queries and Python functions (Li et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2025; Zhuo et al., 2025; Ouyang et al., 2026). These artifacts provide a flexible interface for models to perform computation and interact with external systems (Gao et al., 2023;

Their quality depends not only on the underlying model, but also on the surrounding harness—the prompts, tools, and memory that shape generation (Khattab et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Lopopolo, 2026). This makes the harness a natural target for improving LLM agent performance. Accordingly, existing work has pursued two related directions: optimizing reusable harness components across tasks (Lee et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Agrawal et al., 2026), and using test-time feedback to select or refine generated outputs (Ni et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Madaan et al., 2023). Improving program generation through these directions presents two linked challenges. First, reusable updates must correct recurring errors without degrading behavior that already works. LLM-generated feedback can be unreliable without external grounding (Huang et al., 2024; Kamoi et al., 2024), and prompt revisions that resolve failures can introduce regressions on previously successful cases (Wu et al., 2024b). The challenge is therefore to derive grounded diagnoses of what to change and preserve from execution outcomes, and translate these diagnoses into reusable guidance. Second, this general guidance must be complemented by feedback specific to the current instance. An optimized prompt captures strategies learned across training tasks, but a generated program may still encounter errors that require observations from its own execution. Approaches such as Dynamic Cheatsheet (DC) and ACE accumulate experience through evolving shared contexts (Suzgun et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). When shared context is updated at test time, unreliable or overly specific feedback can become persistent guidance, allowing errors from one instance to affect subsequent tasks. tivate grounding offline harness updates in execution evidence while keeping test-time corrections local to the current program. To address these challenges, we introduce HERO (Harnessing Evidence for Refinement and Optimization), a two-level framework that grounds reusable guidance updates in execution evidence and confines test-time adaptation to the current program. Our contributions are threefold:

• A unified two-level formulation. We formulate program generation as a twolevel optimization problem that couples offline prompt optimization with testtime refinement of instance-specific programs.

• Execution-grounded feedback and verification. Offline, we use execution evidence from successful and failed programs under prior prompts to identify what to correct and preserve. At test time, execution feedback and retrieved verified training examples guide program revisions, which are accepted only when supported by evidence.

• Empirical evaluation and analysis. We demonstrate correctness gains over existing offline harness optimizers across diverse query-generation and programming tasks, with further improvements from test-time refinement. We further evaluate execution eﬀiciency and computational cost, finding that the learned prompts remain compact across tasks.

## 2 Related Works

Prompt and harness optimization. Prompt and harness optimization improves frozen LLMs by adapting reusable components around them. MIPRO (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024) jointly optimizes instructions and few-shot demonstrations using task-level feedback. Reflection-based approaches include GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026), which uses trajectory feedback to propose prompt revisions, and STRAGO (Wu et al., 2024b), which derives refinement strategies from both successful and failed examples to mitigate prompt drift. Other approaches broaden

the optimization target: ACE (Zhang et al., 2026) maintains an evolving context through generation, reflection, and curation; SkillOpt (Yang et al., 2026) optimizes reusable textual skills; and Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) searches over harness implementations using source code, scores, and execution traces. Building on this line of work, HERO adopts a similar offline optimization loop but enriches reflection with execution feedback from successful and failed programs generated under prior prompt revisions, aiming to improve program generation while limiting regressions. Test-time refinement. Test-time methods refine model outputs using feedback available during inference. ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) interleaves reasoning, actions, and environment observations, while Reflexion and related self-refinement methods use feedback from earlier attempts to revise subsequent outputs (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023). Dynamic Cheatsheet (DC) (Suzgun et al., 2026) further accumulates self-curated strategies across queries through persistent memory. These methods emphasize adaptation from test-time experience. HERO complements this adaptation with reusable guidance learned through offline prompt optimization. The optimized prompt remains fixed during inference, while execution feedback and retrieved, verified training examples guide refinement of the current program.

4.1.1 Textual Gradients from Execution-grounded Experience Prompt optimization can be viewed as a discrete analogue of gradient-based optimization, where natural language critiques or reflections serve as “textual gradients” for prompt updates (Pryzant et al., 2023; Yuksekgonul et al., 2024). Prior work uses LLM reflection to guide prompt updates (Pryzant et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2026; Agrawal et al., 2026), but such feedback can be unreliable without external grounding (Huang et al., 2024; Kamoi et al., 2024). Following Wu et al. (2024b), we use both successful and failed cases but enrich reflection with execution outcomes and traces from programs generated under prior prompt revisions to identify what to correct and preserve. 4.1.2 Adaptive Paired Acceptance Prior work has explored bandit-based candidate selection (Pryzant et al., 2023) and minibatch comparisons of prompt revisions against their parent prompts (Agrawal et al., 2026). ### 4.2 HERO-T: Evidence-Grounded Test-Time Refinement

Stage 2 of HERO adapts the instance-specific harness while keeping the learned shared prompt fixed. Given a test instance 𝑥, we first generate

We then refine this program for at most 𝐵 steps using only evidence available at test time, without access to the test solution or correctness label.

4.2.1 Two Sources of Refinement Evidence Refinement draws on two complementary sources. Execution evidence includes execution traces, runtime errors, returned outputs, and environment probes that help identify instance-specific problems. Retrieved demonstration evidence consists of execution-verified training examples that provide implementation patterns, such as library-specific conventions, that execution feedback alone may not reveal. The refiner combines environment interaction and execution-based program refinement (Yao et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2024) with instance-specific demonstration retrieval. Unlike MIPROv2, which selects demonstrations during offline optimization (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024), we select demonstrations separately for each test instance. Specifically, we retrieve up to 𝑛verified training examples using lexical similarity, then let the refiner select at most three relevant demonstrations.

## 5 Experimental Setup

### 5.1 Benchmarks

We evaluate on four text-to-function generation benchmarks spanning SQL, Cypher, and Python generation. BIRD-SQL (Li et al., 2023). BIRD-SQL evaluates text-to-SQL generation over realistic SQLite databases from diverse application domains. Given a natural-language question, database schema, and optional external knowledge, the model generates an executable SQL query. CypherBench (Feng et al., 2025). Cypher- Bench evaluates text-to-Cypher generation over large-scale Neo4j property graphs derived from Wikidata, covering query patterns such

### 5.2 Models and Baselines

We compare against three classes of methods: (i) offline prompt optimization1, including GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026), MIPROv2 (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024), ACE (Zhang et al., 2026), and SkillOpt (Yang et al., 2026); (ii) test-time refinement, including ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) and Dynamic Cheatsheet (DC- Cu) (Suzgun et al., 2026); and (iii) end-toend harness optimization, represented by Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026). Offline optimizers start from the same seed prompt (Section G) and use the same optimization data and execution-based correctness signal. Testtime methods use only information available at inference time, without access to reference solutions, reference outputs, or correctness labels. For each benchmark, we set a fixed rollout budget based on GEPA’s auto=heavy setting (Table 4) and apply the same budget to HERO and all baselines, matching rollout counts as closely as their procedures permit. ## 7 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced HERO, a twostage harness framework for program generation that combines grounded offline prompt optimization with evidence-grounded testtime refinement. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, HERO consistently outperforms the initial prompt and existing prompt optimization baselines, with test-time refinement providing further gains on every benchmark. Our analyses show that executiongrounded updates reduce regressions during optimization, while the learned prompts remain compact and robust across optimization settings. Together, these results support combining reusable cross-task optimization with instance-specific refinement for more effective program generation.

## Limitations

Budgeting and computational cost. Our evaluation uses fixed, benchmark-specific budgets, which may limit the gains that some methods could achieve with longer searches. Substantially expanding these budgets is computationally demanding: even under the evaluated budgets, ACE and Meta-Harness require approximately 12 and 24 hours of wallclock time, respectively, on BigCodeBench in our setup. To support controlled comparisons within these practical constraints, we use taskrollout counts as a common measure of evaluation effort and match budgets as closely as method-specific procedures permit. This measure, however, does not fully capture differences in the costs of reflection, candidate generation, and selection. Nevertheless, we have sought to make the comparisons as fair and

## A Datasets Details

Here, we provide additional details on each benchmark and our preprocessing and splitting procedures. Three conventions apply across all datasets. First, all splits are constructed once using a fixed dataset-level seed before any experiment, and pool membership is held fixed across methods and run seeds. Second, the diagnosis pool 𝒟diag, update pool 𝒟upd, and, when applicable, selection pool 𝒟sel are disjoint at the instance level. BIRD-SQL (Li et al., 2023). BIRD-SQL is a large-scale text-to-SQL benchmark designed to evaluate SQL generation in realistic database settings, where models must reason over database contents in addition to schemas. It contains 12,751 natural-language– SQL pairs across 95 SQLite databases and 37 application domains: 9,428 training examples over 69 databases, 1,534 development examples over 11 databases, and 1,789 examples over 15 databases in a concealed test set. Among the training and development databases, 32% originate from Kaggle, 48% from the CTU Prague Relational Learning Repository, and the remaining 20% from other publicly available tables. Each instance includes a natural-language question, a reference SQL query, the associated database, and optional expert-annotated external knowledge. The development set spans three diﬀiculty levels: 925 simple, 465 moderate, and 144 challenging examples, categorized based on question understanding, external knowledge requirements, database complexity, and SQL complexity. BIRD also evaluates execution efficiency, enabling assessment of both correctness and runtime behavior.

Preprocessing and splits. Following StreamBench (Wu et al., 2024a), we use the oﬀicial TRAIN split for optimization and the oﬀicial DEV split for evaluation, both downloaded from 2; the concealed test set is not used. To evaluate cross-database transfer, we partition TRAIN at the database level. We reserve 14 of the 69 training databases for final prompt selection, sampling at most 100 questions per database. Of the remaining 55 databases, 15 are reserved exclusively for the update pool, from which we sample 250 questions, while the 500-question diagnosis pool is sampled from the remaining 40 databases with every database represented. Thus, the diagnosis, update, and selection pools are disjoint at the database level. Before sampling, we exclude examples whose reference queries fail to execute or return empty results. For final evaluation, we use the 1,534 DEV examples and exclude four whose reference queries fail under our evaluator, yielding 1,530 scored examples. Correctness is determined using the oﬀicial executionaccuracy comparator: predicted and reference outputs are compared as sets of tuples, ignoring row order and duplicates while preserving column order.

C.1 Offline Prompt Optimization

We run 𝑇= 5 optimization rounds with no early stopping. In each round, we evaluate the current prompt on the full diagnosis set and uniformly sample 32 incorrect and 32 correct examples. For incorrect examples, the reflector receives the task input, generated output, failure category, evaluator feedback, and available reference information; correct examples are included to identify behaviors that should be preserved. The optimization context also includes aggregate failure statistics and complementary feedback from the previous round. Based on this information, the reflector independently proposes four candidate prompt revisions, with up to eight edits per candidate. Proposals are rejected if they cannot be parsed, leave the prompt unchanged, or introduce task-specific values or identifiers found only in reference solutions.

Candidate evaluation and acceptance. In each optimization round, we compare four candidate prompts with the current prompt using adaptive paired evaluation (Algorithm 2). All candidates are initially evaluated on the same 50 examples from the 250-example update set, with a budget of two additional 50- example pulls allocated by the algorithm. Candidate scores are paired improvements in execution accuracy, macro-averaged across observed databases or domains. Standard errors are computed from the sample standard deviation of group means divided by the square root of the number of observed groups, floored by the pooled row-level standard error with minimum per-row variance 0.02. We set 𝑧= 1 for evaluation allocation and early stopping, but accept an update only if the best candidate’s estimated mean improvement exceeds 𝜏= 0.01. Accepted prompts and any additional candidates exceeding this threshold are archived for final selection.

Final selection. After five optimization rounds, we select the final prompt through a second adaptive race over the archive, with a budget equal to 75% of the evaluations needed to score every archived prompt on the full selection set.

C.2 Test-Time Refinement

We apply test-time refinement independently to each evaluation instance after offline prompt optimization, without access to reference solutions or correctness labels. Each episode starts from the initial output generated by the selected offline prompt; therefore, 𝐵= 0 recovers the corresponding unrefined prediction. Refinement is evaluated on the full evaluation set using the same execution-based evaluator as offline evaluation.

Tools and interaction budget. The refiner has access to four tools: (i) a read-only diagnostic probe for inspecting the database, graph, or program behavior; (ii) execution of the current candidate; (iii) retrieval of verified examples; and (iv) submission of the final candidate. We use an interaction budget of 𝐵= 3, counting diagnostic, execution, and retrieval actions; final submission does not consume the budget. Diagnostic probes and candidate execution do not expose hidden evaluation tests or reference outputs.

Verified-example retrieval. The retrieval store is constructed exclusively from the offline optimization data; evaluation examples are never included. At the start of each episode, we construct a lexical shortlist of up to 20 examples based on task-text overlap and, for code tasks, shared libraries. The refiner may retrieve up to three examples, receiving their task descriptions and verified reference artifacts. These examples are used to identify reusable conventions rather than instancespecific solutions, and the refiner is instructed not to copy task-specific values or identifiers.

Refinement and verification. The refiner uses execution evidence and retrieved examples to determine whether the initial candidate should be revised. Retrieval-based revisions require consistent evidence for a relevant convention, while execution-based revisions must be supported by observations from the current
